question.prompt: There exists a unique strictly increasing sequence of nonnegative integers \(a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_k\) such that \[\frac{2^{289}+1}{2^{17}+1}=2^{a_1}+2^{a_2}+\cdots+2^{a_k}.\] What is \(k?\)

solutions.title: Expand into blocks of powers
solutions.explanation:
The number \(k\) counts the \(1\)-digits in the quotient's binary expansion. Since \(289=17\cdot17\), setting \(X=2^{17}\) lets us find those digits without computing the enormous quotient.

We have
\[
\frac{2^{289}+1}{2^{17}+1}
=\frac{X^{17}+1}{X+1}
=X^{16}-X^{15}+X^{14}-X^{13}+\cdots+X^2-X+1.
\]
To verify the last equality, multiply the alternating sum by \(X+1\). All intermediate powers cancel, leaving \(X^{17}+1\).

Group the terms into eight differences and the final \(1\):
\[
(X^{16}-X^{15})+(X^{14}-X^{13})+\cdots+(X^2-X)+1.
\]
Each difference has the form \(X^{m+1}-X^m\), where \(m\) is one of \(1,3,5,\ldots,15\). Since
\[
2^{17}-1=1+2+2^2+\cdots+2^{16},
\]
we get
\[
X^{m+1}-X^m
=2^{17m}(2^{17}-1)
=2^{17m}+2^{17m+1}+\cdots+2^{17m+16}.
\]
Thus each difference contributes \(17\) distinct powers of \(2\).

The exponent intervals are
\[
17\text{ through }33,\quad 51\text{ through }67,\quad\ldots,\quad255\text{ through }271.
\]
They do not overlap, so adding the blocks creates no binary carries. The final \(1=2^0\) supplies one more distinct power.

Therefore \(k=8\cdot17+1=\boxed{137}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Track binary carries
solutions.explanation:
Multiplication by \(2^{17}+1\) adds a number to a copy shifted \(17\) binary places. Tracking this addition reveals which digits of the quotient are \(1\).

Call the quotient \(N\). We need
\[
N+2^{17}N=2^{289}+1.
\]
Number binary positions starting at \(0\), so position \(i\) has value \(2^i\). The required sum has a \(1\) only in positions \(0\) and \(289\).

At position \(0\), the digit of \(N\) must be \(1\). Its digits in positions \(1\) through \(16\) must be \(0\), since the shifted copy has not yet contributed.

At position \(17\), the shifted copy contributes the original position-\(0\) digit, which is \(1\). To make the sum's digit \(0\), the digit of \(N\) must also be \(1\). Their sum is \(2\), which writes a \(0\) and carries \(1\) to the next position.

In positions \(18\) through \(33\), the shifted digits are \(0\). Each incoming carry is \(1\), so the corresponding digit of \(N\) must be \(1\), again producing a \(0\) and another carry.

After that, each column still has an incoming carry of \(1\). To produce a sum digit of \(0\), the digit of \(N\) must be opposite to the digit \(17\) places earlier: choose \(0\) when the shifted digit is \(1\), and \(1\) when it is \(0\). Each column totals \(2\), so the carry continues. This produces alternating blocks of \(17\) zeros and \(17\) ones.

The blocks of ones occupy positions
\[
17+34j\text{ through }33+34j,\qquad j=0,1,\ldots,7.
\]
The last such block ends at \(271\), followed by zeros in positions \(272\) through \(288\). At position \(289\), both number digits are \(0\), and the incoming carry supplies the required final \(1\). Taking all higher digits to be zero completes the required addition.

Thus \(N\) has eight blocks of \(17\) ones and the lone one at position \(0\). Therefore \(k=8\cdot17+1=\boxed{137}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
